name: Nikhil Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary site day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Nikhil Abbott, 43, and I fit interior doors and do general trades in low-rise apartment buildings. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of work, so ordinary frames are familiar, but I still ask the lead about an unusual fire door. I have never used AI. This small builder pays below the usual rate and cuts hours in winter, and there are few other site employers nearby.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the situation at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner takes part-time home-care shifts, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. A boiler repair left us with about three weeks of expenses saved. A quiet week at the apartments can undo what we put aside the month before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apartment crew that an office tool may file the door orders faster, but a door still has to clear an uneven floor. I have never used AI and do not want a phone guessing at a fire door. Give me the right hinge schedule and enough time to fit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and know my way around a normal interior fit-out, but the local builder pays poorly and winter hours drop. My partner works part-time in home care, and we have three weeks of bills saved after a boiler repair. The mortgage does not ease because AI turns out mild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid door-fitting shift and ask the site lead on Wednesday which rooms are ready next week. In the first year I would keep packing lunch instead of buying it near the site. I would also ask the supplier to replace any wrong hinges before cutting a frame to suit a bad delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the hours. The technology story barely moves the needle, but a two-day week does. I do not want to explain another late mortgage payment to the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the boiler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It failed just as the last apartment block finished, so we paid the repair bill from the savings account. My partner picked up an extra home-care shift, but the account is still under a month of bills. That made the next quiet week feel longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why worry about hinges?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supplier once sent the wrong closing hinge for a fire door. I put the box aside and rang the site lead before fitting anything. Rework would have taken the afternoon and might have left the door unsafe.

say: I would say faster **door orders** do not correct an uneven floor.
I would insist on the right **fire-door hinges** before fitting.
think: I have a **trade certificate**, yet low pay and short winter weeks strain the mortgage.
A boiler repair left only **three weeks saved**.
do: Keep every paid **door-fitting shift** and ask which rooms are ready.
Pack **site lunches** instead of buying food near the job.
Return **wrong hinges** before altering a frame.
feel: **Anxious** about short weeks even when AI changes little.
S0.quote: The technology story barely moves the needle, but a two-day week does.
fieldNote: Nikhil’s recent **boiler bill** explains why a skilled worker has such a thin reserve.
His fire-door example shows **practical caution** rooted in safety, without any current AI use.

steps.text: Keep paid door-fitting shifts and ask which rooms are ready next week
Pack lunches instead of buying food near the building site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office might book doors and check orders faster, and that could spare us bad deliveries. I would ask whether the contractor plans to pay for a full fitting day if the new schedule compresses jobs. The crew needs a written roster, not a cheerful screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical fitting is still mine for now, but the builder could run fewer fitters across the same flats. Lower winter pay already stretches us, and home-care hours for my partner change at short notice. If either wage shrinks, our three-week reserve will go quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting doors and write down every cancelled room and lost hour for two months. If the roster gets shorter, I'd call the regional renovation firm about paid vacancies and ask my partner whether an early commute could work with school pickup. In the first year I'd cut the children's paid weekend outings before touching the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the office change and anxious about the budget. I would gladly avoid a wrong hinge delivery. I need the saved time to turn into paid work, not an empty Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far is the regional firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About an hour each way by car. That is a hard trip when my partner is on an early care visit, so we would need a pickup plan. I would call about a real wage before spending fuel on an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why log the cancelled rooms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a flat was not ready and the supervisor said the day would be moved, but it never appeared on my payslip. A dated list lets me ask a straight question. I am not looking for a fight; I want to be paid for days promised.

say: I would ask whether **faster booking** still provides a full paid fitting day.
I would demand a **written roster** for the crew.
think: A smaller fitter crew could shrink my **winter wage**.
My partner’s changing **care hours** and three-week reserve leave little margin.
do: Keep paid **door work** and log lost fitting hours for two months.
Call the **regional renovation firm** if the roster contracts.
Cut paid **weekend outings** before missing mortgage payments.
feel: **Anxious** about household income despite welcoming fewer wrong deliveries.
S1.quote: I need the saved time to turn into paid work, not an empty Thursday.
fieldNote: He checks **actual paid hours** rather than opposing faster ordering in principle.
The regional fallback entails a **one-hour commute** and school pickup coordination, so it depends on a real wage.

steps.text: Keep paid door shifts and log cancelled room hours for two months
Call the regional renovation firm if paid roster days shrink
Cut paid family weekend outings before touching mortgage payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the planning desk changes by 2028, and robots able to fit doors arrive around 2031. I would ask the builder when it expects to use those machines on occupied flats. A showroom door is not a fire door in a crooked opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the thinking change and 48 when robots can do hands-on fitting. With three weeks saved and few nearby employers, I expect a big loss of income if the builder replaces its fitters. I have caught myself awake at night counting the mortgage payments before 2031. My partner's home-care work may face capable robots then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid shift and ask the builder for a written staffing and trial timetable. This month I'd ring the regional renovation firm and send an application if it has paid openings; that work could also change by 2031, but it might keep money coming. In the first year after 2028 we'd stop saving for a new television and ask my sister to cover one school pickup if a regional interview lands on a care shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make a call, but a short warning does not give us money to wait. I would be frightened of both household jobs changing before the boiler fund is rebuilt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fire-door example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rated door has to close and seal in a real opening. I would want to see the robot fit one in an old flat and have a qualified person sign it off. Until then, a demonstration in a clean showroom tells me little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask her for one pickup, not for cash. She has helped when my partner had an early home-care visit. If a regional employer offers a paid job, family time could help us take it.

say: I would tell coworkers **2028 desk AI** comes before 2031 door-fitting robots.
I would ask for a **real fire-door trial** and staffing dates.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots could do my fitting work.
Three weeks saved, few local jobs and possible **two-wage loss** keep me awake.
do: Keep every paid **fitting shift** and ask for a written robot timetable.
Apply to the **regional renovation firm** if paid vacancies exist.
Drop the **new television fund** and ask my sister for pickup if an interview comes.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely major income loss and little time to rebuild savings.
S2.quote: A showroom door is not a fire door in a crooked opening.
fieldNote: Nikhil expects a **major wage risk** around 2031 and explicitly describes sleepless mortgage counting.
His regional application is for **current paid work**, not a claim that renovation remains safe after capable robots.

steps.text: Keep paid fitting shifts and request a written robot timetable
Apply to the regional renovation firm if paid openings exist
Stop setting money aside for a new television
Ask his sister for school pickup if a regional interview conflicts with care shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office changes by 2031 and capable site robots arrive around 2034. Five years gives the builder time to test a machine in an old flat and tell workers what it found. I would not accept a promise based on an empty showroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might have fewer winter hours anyway, but at 51 a robot could fit the doors I know how to handle. The children will be older, yet the mortgage may still run. Five years is more useful than two only if we can rebuild some savings in paid weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting doors and ask the lead to give me more difficult fire-door frames to practice under supervision. If the builder offers paid training on checking robot-fitted doors, I'd attend only after seeing a safe trial. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply to regional builders that still have paid fittings and put any rare overtime toward the boiler fund before buying anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less trapped than in the fast picture. I have time to find out what local firms really do. I still need a full week's pay long before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a checking role be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. A robot able to fit a fire door may also check the seal, so I would not bet the mortgage on that title. Paid training would be useful only if the builder has real shifts for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as rebuilding the fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I would get a full month of bills back into the account after the boiler repair. If overtime arrives, I would put it there before replacing the television. We cannot afford a long course fee right now.

say: I would ask for **old-flat trials** before 2034 fitting robots arrive.
I would demand results beyond an **empty showroom**.
think: I would be **51** when robots can fit doors as well as workers.
Five years helps only if paid weeks rebuild the **boiler fund**.
do: Keep paid **door shifts** and practice difficult fire frames with the lead.
Attend **paid robot-check training** if a safe trial and real shifts exist.
Apply to **regional builders** after 2031 and put overtime into the emergency account.
feel: **Anxious**, though the longer warning allows some checks and applications.
S3.quote: Paid training would be useful only if the builder has real shifts for it.
fieldNote: Nikhil makes **paid shifts** a condition for robot-check training and doubts that checking stays human work.
The **boiler fund** gives his savings goal a concrete one-month first target.

steps.text: Keep paid door shifts and practice difficult fire frames under supervision
Attend paid robot-check training only after a safe trial and confirmed shifts
Apply to paid regional fitting jobs after 2031 if advertised
Put any overtime into the emergency account until one month of bills is saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office changes by 2036 and hands-on robots reach fitting around 2039. A decade is time to ask for real trials and learn from paid work, not a reason to ignore short winter weeks now. I would want the contractor's dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the desk change and 56 when robots can do my physical work. Our children will be grown, so school pickup will not bind us to this town the same way. I still cannot assume a pension or a paid-off mortgage with our current rate and thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid apartment work and ask for a winter roster early each year. My partner and I would put any overtime first into a one-month reserve, then toward the mortgage. In the first year after 2036 I would compare real robot trial results with what the builder says and ask the regional firm about paid openings if local days fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the coming winter, even with a long robot warning. A decade gives the children time to grow and us more choices about commuting. It does not put an extra day on next week's payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move once the children are grown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could consider a longer commute first. Selling a house for a job that might vanish would be a large risk. I would need a written offer and a clear mortgage plan before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reliable four- or five-day roster and prompt pay when a room is cancelled. That would let us rebuild the emergency account after the boiler. A robot plan is useful later, but this winter’s hours are the immediate bill.

say: I would ask for **written dates** for 2039 fitting robots.
I would keep pushing for **winter shifts** now.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and a possible mortgage.
I cannot assume **pension income** or enough savings to stop earning.
do: Keep paid **apartment work** and request an early winter roster.
Build a **one-month reserve** from overtime before extra mortgage payments.
Check **regional paid openings** after 2036 if local days fall.
feel: Still **anxious** about near-term winter pay despite a distant robot date.
S4.quote: A robot plan is useful later, but this winter’s hours are the immediate bill.
fieldNote: Nikhil separates the **2039 robot date** from the coming winter’s urgent pay gap.
Grown children may loosen the **commuting constraint**, while moving still requires a written job offer.

steps.text: Keep paid apartment work and ask early for the winter roster
Put overtime into an emergency account until one month of bills is saved
Ask the regional firm about paid openings after 2036 if local days fall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots reach door fitting around 2031, with few local builders to turn to. A written trial timetable, honest paid-vacancy information and reliable winter shifts would help. I can drive farther for a real wage, but I cannot move the family for a rumour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a worker rebuilds savings after an ordinary house repair. The boiler took our cushion before any robot appeared. A steady roster now would make every future plan more possible.

headlineQuote: The boiler took our cushion before any robot appeared.
portrait: Nikhil is a **43-year-old certified** door fitter with experienced, average skills on low-rise apartment sites.
Low winter pay, variable **home-care shifts** and a boiler repair leave three weeks saved for two children and a mortgage.
He has **never used AI** and wants fire-door work checked on real, uneven openings.
He seeks **paid regional work** and a rebuilt emergency fund before making any move based on robot forecasts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable door-fitting robots around 2031 to an area with few alternative builders.
whatWouldHelp: A written **trial timetable**, real vacancies and reliable winter shifts would help him protect household wages.
